query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A coating made from an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high‐entropy alloy (HEA) can be effectively applied to a copper matrix to improve its wear resistance because its intrinsic high hardness and oxide‐forming behavior enable the development of a protective, self‐lubricating scale, while spark plasma sintering (SPS) processing promotes strong metallurgical bonding with copper.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) substrate with a clean, pre-treated surface prepared for coating.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin layer of atomised AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA powder onto the Cu matrix using spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating wear tests conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to around 900 °C) in an air atmosphere to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, protective oxide layer (e.g., spinel or Cr-rich oxides) on the HEA surface combined with a fine-grained SPS microstructure that bonds well to Cu.
generation.mechanism: During wear, the HEA coating’s high hardness resists material removal while tribo-oxidation leads to the formation of a protective oxide layer that lowers friction. Additionally, the SPS process facilitates interfacial diffusion and metallurgical bonding between the HEA and the copper substrate, ensuring strong adhesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA-coated Cu substrate will show significantly reduced wear rates and lower friction coefficients compared to bare copper, with the coating remaining adherent throughout the wear tests.
generation.baseline: Bare copper exhibits relatively high wear rates and poor oxidation resistance, leading to rapid surface degradation under tribological loading.
generation.boundary: If the processing conditions induce excessive thermal stresses or if the coefficient of thermal expansion mismatch between the HEA and Cu is too large, interfacial delamination might occur, compromising performance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal SPS processing parameters for achieving a defect-free, strongly bonded interface between the HEA coating and the Cu substrate, as well as the long-term interfacial stability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group consisting of copper substrates coated with the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA via SPS, and a control group of bare copper substrates. Subject both groups to identical reciprocating wear tests under room temperature and elevated temperature conditions (up to 900 °C). Monitor the evolution of wear rates, friction coefficients, and interfacial integrity throughout the test using surface imaging and adhesion tests.
measurements: Interfacial adhesion strength (via scratch or pull-off tests)
Microstructural analysis of the coating-substrate interface using SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated copper does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction (or if it shows premature delamination at the interface) compared to the uncoated control under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C. Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h.
